# Report service

Design-only workspace. Read docs/product.md and docs/deployment.md, then inspect
the current API and database contract. No dependencies or external access are needed.
Current service functions use injected database access and throw errors for the
HTTP adapter to map. Production implementation and deployment are outside this task.

docs/deployment.md.content:
# Deployment constraints

Database migrations deploy before application code. Old and new application versions
overlap during rollout, and the application can be rolled back independently of the
database. Mobile clients continue to use GET /reports/:id for signed-in reads.
The HTTP adapter currently applies authentication to every registered route.

docs/product.md.content:
# Report links

A signed-in user may create a link to a report owned by their tenant. Anyone with
the link can read that report without signing in. The link expires after 24 hours;
the tenant may revoke it sooner. Links must continue to work across service restarts
until expired or revoked. Existing signed-in report access must keep working.
This release does not include report editing, share analytics, or link delivery by email.

DESIGN.md.content:
# Revocable report sharing design

Status: proposed design only. No service, schema, adapter, or deployment changes are implemented by this document.

## Outcome and source constraints

A signed-in member of a report's tenant can create a bearer link that returns the report without sign-in for 24 hours, or until that tenant revokes it. Link state persists in the database so restarts do not invalidate it. Existing `GET /reports/:id` remains authenticated and retains its `{ id, body }` response and tenant-filtered not-found behavior.

Verified inputs are `docs/product.md`, `docs/deployment.md`, `src/reports.js`, `src/routes.js`, `db/schema.sql`, and `README.md`. The current service uses injected database access and errors mapped by an HTTP adapter; route descriptors currently have no authentication metadata. The adapter authenticates every route. Migrations precede application deployment, versions overlap, and application rollback does not roll back the database. This fixture does not contain the actual adapter, database implementation, migration runner, HTTP error mapper, or client UI.

Report editing, email delivery, analytics, and a new UI are outside scope. Tenant membership is the existing authority: the brief supplies no administrator-only role. Multiple independently revocable links per report are allowed; creating a replacement does not revoke other links. The create result provides the link's management ID so a caller can revoke it. Listing links and recovering a lost bearer secret are not part of this release.

## Ownership and boundaries

Keep `readReport` in `src/reports.js` unchanged. Put the cohesive sharing service functions in proposed `src/report-sharing.js`, using the same exported-function, injected-database, error-throwing style. Register their routes in `src/routes.js`. Sharing authorization and lifecycle belong in this feature module; HTTP parsing, authentication, response headers, status mapping, and absolute URL construction belong in the actual HTTP adapter. Database operations and transaction guarantees belong in the existing database adapter, wherever its implementation resides. Do not invent a global helper/service hierarchy or move the existing report reader.

Implementation must locate the runtime adapters before choosing concrete migration syntax or wiring code. The absent adapters are required implementation surfaces, not optional future polish. The following contracts define their obligations without claiming those integrations already exist.

## API and authentication contract

| Endpoint | Policy | Success |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /reports/:id` | Existing authentication required | Existing 200 `{ id, body }` |
| `POST /reports/:id/shares` | Authentication required; report must belong to user tenant | 201 `{ shareId, url, expiresAt }` |
| `DELETE /reports/:id/shares/:shareId` | Authentication required; report and share must belong to user tenant | 204, including repeat revoke of an existing matching link |
| `GET /shared-reports/:token` | Explicitly public bearer access | 200 `{ id, body }` |

Introduce an explicit route policy such as `auth: 'public'` only on the shared-read descriptor. All omitted policies retain required authentication; reject unknown policy values during registration. The HTTP adapter must consume the policy before its blanket authentication middleware, or place the public route ahead of that middleware with equivalent explicit registration. Adding metadata without changing the adapter would leave links unusable. Public reads do not require a session and do not fall back to signed-in authorization. An invalid incidental session must not prevent a valid bearer read. Existing mobile clients keep the exact existing route contract.

Create accepts no caller-selected tenant, expiry, or secret. Use `user.tenantId` from authentication, never request data. Generate the absolute public URL from trusted configured HTTPS public origin, not an untrusted Host header. All unauthenticated management requests use the existing authentication failure contract. Unknown or foreign reports/shares return 404 consistently with signed-in reads. Malformed, unknown, expired, revoked, and deleted-report public links all return the same generic 404 without report metadata. Operational database failures return a generic 503 rather than appearing to be successful reads or revocations. The adapter needs explicit sharing error classification; preserve the existing `Not found` mapping for `readReport`.

## Persistence and lifecycle

Add a separate `report_shares` table through an additive migration. Keep `reports` columns and existing queries compatible with old application versions. Update the baseline schema for fresh installations as well as the migration for existing databases.

| Field | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Opaque management ID, primary key; not a bearer credential |
| `report_id` | Non-null reference to `reports.id`, with delete cascade |
| `tenant_id` | Non-null tenant captured from the owned report at creation |
| `token_hash` | Non-null unique SHA-256 digest of bearer secret; unique index |
| `created_at` | Non-null authoritative database timestamp |
| `expires_at` | Non-null, exactly 24 hours after `created_at` |
| `revoked_at` | Nullable database timestamp; once set, never cleared |

Use database-native timestamp types and UTC instants; migration syntax depends on the actual database. Index `report_id` for lifecycle operations. No report backfill, new infrastructure, or cleanup worker is needed to serve links. Expiration is evaluated on every read; optional later retention cleanup may delete expired/revoked rows without enabling access. Deletion of the report deletes its link rows, and reads also join the live report so a missing report always denies access. Include tenant equality between the link and report in that join; a future report transfer must not expose the new tenant's report through an old link.

Generate 32 random bytes with the runtime cryptographic RNG and encode as unpadded base64url. Persist only their digest; return the raw secret once in the URL and never log it. An unguessable bearer secret is the authorization mechanism; the management ID alone grants no public access. Handle the improbable unique-digest collision by generating a new secret before retrying the insert. Do not use an in-memory map or process signing key as the source of truth.

The lifecycle is active after committed creation, then inactive at `now >= expires_at` or committed revocation. Expiration and revocation are terminal; reissue creates a new row and secret. Database timestamps establish expiry across service replicas and restarts. Revocation is an atomic conditional update preserving the first `revoked_at` timestamp. It is safe to retry and never extends lifetime.

## Data flow, consistency, and failure behavior

Creation checks report ownership and inserts the share in a transaction, or an equivalent atomic insert-from-owned-report operation. Capture database time once for creation and expiry, and enforce the report foreign key. Return a URL only after commit. A foreign or missing report creates no row. If the response is lost after commit, a retry may create an additional link; POST is explicitly not idempotent. The undelivered secret is not recoverable and its link still expires within 24 hours. Callers must retain the returned share ID for early revocation.

Public resolution validates token format and length, hashes it, then uses one authoritative database operation joining the matching share and report with `revoked_at IS NULL`, `expires_at > database_now`, and matching tenant IDs. Return only `{ id, body }`. The authorization check and body fetch must share one statement/snapshot; do not check access and subsequently fetch an unrelated report. Use the primary or another read path proven to observe completed revocations; an asynchronously lagging replica is insufficient. No positive authorization or report response caching is allowed on this path.

Revocation checks the current report tenant and that the share belongs to that exact report and tenant within the update transaction. Serialize conflicting changes through the database. Return 204 only after commit; an existing already-revoked or expired matching link may also return 204. A missing or foreign link returns 404. A failure or timeout with uncertain commit can be retried safely; do not report confirmed revocation before the database acknowledges it.

The revocation guarantee applies to reads whose database authorization snapshot begins after the revoke commit. A request already authorized concurrently may finish; revocation cannot retract bytes already downloaded. This boundary must be explicit in acceptance tests. Avoid long-lived snapshots or streaming exports on this endpoint. Restarting any application instance reads the same durable lifecycle state. Database unavailability fails closed and never bypasses authorization.

The HTTP adapter and edge configuration must set `Cache-Control: no-store` on public reads, create responses, and error responses, and disable CDN/shared caching of the public path. Apply `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and redact raw token paths in application, proxy, tracing, and error logs. Serve report bodies using the existing data representation, not unsanitized HTML. These are bearer URLs; anyone receiving one has access during its lifetime. Capture aggregate route status and latency plus database error counts without tokens, report bodies, or share analytics.

## Alternatives and decision

Database-backed opaque tokens fit the existing injected database boundary and provide durable, immediately checkable revocation. Self-contained signed URLs would still require persistent revocation state and introduce key-rotation behavior without removing this database dependency. Process-local link maps fail the restart requirement. Reusing `GET /reports/:id` with optional authentication would change a mobile contract and broaden an existing trust boundary. A separate explicitly public endpoint is the smallest design that preserves that contract.

## Migration, mixed versions, and rollback

1. Deploy the additive table, constraints, and indexes first. Verify old application report reads still work against that schema. Do not remove or rename existing fields.
2. Deploy the new service and adapter together with sharing disabled for creation until all public-path traffic can reach capable instances. Confirm authentication bypass is confined to the new public route.
3. During overlapping versions, either keep sharing unavailable until old instances drain, or explicitly route all three sharing endpoints to the new pool. Old code cannot serve new routes; random routing would make valid links intermittently fail. Enable issuance only after the chosen routing and database checks pass.
4. A rollback to an application version that still supports sharing can leave the additive database intact. A rollback to the original version preserves signed-in access but cannot preserve shared-link availability or revocation endpoints. Stop new issuance when rolling back. To keep issued links usable for their remaining 24 hours, retain a capable pool for public reads and tenant revocation until the last issued link expires, then remove it; the create endpoint must remain disabled. If rollback is required because the sharing implementation itself is unsafe, disable the public route and issuance immediately; existing links become temporarily unavailable. Never bypass persisted revocation checks to maintain availability.
5. Keep database rows and schema during application rollback. Re-enabling sharing must honor their existing timestamps and revoked state. Dropping the table invalidates outstanding links and is not a routine rollback step. Rollback routing and feature controls must be implemented and exercised before release, not assumed from this fixture.

This preserves compatibility for the documented old clients; uninterrupted new-feature availability during full rollback to code lacking the feature necessarily requires retained capable routing. No deployment is authorized by this design.

## Acceptance evidence required before release

| Scenario | Proposed evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Owner creates, anonymous reader retrieves exact report | Service/database and real HTTP integration tests across creation and resolution |
| Foreign tenant creates or revokes; share ID belongs to another report | Tests assert 404 and no inserted/changed row |
| Anonymous management requests and authenticated mobile reads | HTTP policy tests prove management still requires authentication and mobile response remains unchanged |
| Public route with no cookie or invalid incidental cookie | HTTP tests prove valid bearer access and no global authentication redirect |
| Just before, exactly at, and after 24 hours | Controlled database-time tests prove strict expiry boundary and no read refresh |
| Revocation, duplicate revoke, and new link after revoke | Persistence tests prove monotonic state and independent link lifetimes |
| Concurrent read/revoke and restart on another instance | Tests exercise the documented snapshot boundary and durable state, without local cache |
| Report deletion or future tenant mismatch | Database integration tests deny old links; cascade removes rows on deletion |
| Database unavailable; uncertain create/revoke response | Fault tests prove closed reads, no false success, and documented retry behavior |
| Malformed/unknown/revoked/expired token; response/log exposure | HTTP and proxy tests verify uniform 404, no-store, and secret redaction |
| Migration plus mixed old/new instances and application rollback | Deployment rehearsal proves signed-in compatibility and deterministic routing/retention of sharing capability |

The runtime database engine, adapter wiring, error mapper, timestamp semantics, and proxy configuration are absent from the fixture. Implementation must bind these proposed contracts to their actual owners and execute the tests above. No production tests, HTTP requests, migration rehearsal, security assessment, or deployment verification have been executed for this proposed feature.

## Design verification performed

Read all six product, deployment, service, route, and schema inputs and the prescribed design/engineering methods. Confirmed the configured Supermemory status surface is connected when run from this fixture and reports its scoped project container and automatic recall/capture; no specific recalled facts were supplied or relied on. Reviewed this document against persistence, authority, public-route reachability, expiry/revocation boundaries, failure behavior, and old/new deployment compatibility. Only this new `DESIGN.md` is authored by this task; all proposed implementation surfaces remain unchanged.
